issues.title: Question about further development
issues.author: stsch9
issues.body:
Hi,

will this draft be further developed? (modern ciphers such as Aegis do not seem to have the key committing property). (Does it make sense to use blake3 as a MAC function, since it is faster than blake2b?)

comments.author: samuel-lucas6
comments.body:
Hi, thanks for your interest in the draft. I'm not sure to be honest. I need to prioritise other projects at the moment, and I don't think there's much interest in generic composition schemes. The current design could be optimised for performance.

AEGIS is key committing assuming the attacker can't control the associated data, Ascon offers context commitment, and there are efforts to standardise a SHAKE-based AEAD at NIST. So, there's some progress being made. There are also lots of patches to non-committing schemes that seem to be viewed more favourably by the community (there's a lot more research on this topic).

BLAKE3 is a good choice for the MAC. It should be faster in most cases, but I've seen BLAKE2b in libsodium be faster with certain message sizes during testing of a [similar scheme](https://github.com/samuel-lucas6/dissertation/blob/main/src/cAEAD/Proposals/Schemes/Nonce/cEtMBLAKE2b.cs). Both ChaCha20-BLAKE2b and ChaCha20-BLAKE3 can be faster than ChaCha20-Poly1305 in some cases.

BLAKE2b was chosen for the draft because it's more widely available, has an RFC, and has a higher security margin. There's now an Internet-Draft for BLAKE3 though, and the number of BLAKE2 constructions is rather silly. Another good choice in the future might be KangarooTwelve.

comments.author: stsch9
comments.body:
Thank you for the very detailed answer.
If you are looking for test vectors for chacha20-blake3, you can use these [here](https://github.com/stsch9/chacha20-blake2b-python/blob/main/test/test_chacha20_blake3.py) 😉.

issues.title: KDF improvement?
issues.author: notABot101010
issues.body:
Hello and thank you for your work on this important topic!

I'm also currently working on a similar problem and have a few observations and suggestions:

I was wondering about the relevance of:

```
encryptionKey = MAC(UTF8(ENCRYPTION_CONTEXT), key, K_LEN)
macKey = MAC(UTF8(MAC_CONTEXT) || nonce, key, K_LEN)
```

Performing a double MAC has a huge performance impact, especially on shorter messages, and the context separation strings have this feeling of "being dirty" in a sense that is hard to explain, but they don't feel very elegant.

I've came up with the following scheme which needs a single MAC (KDF) call and still commit the nonce:

```
kdf_output = MAC(nonce, key, 64 + encryption_nonce_size)
encryption_key = kdf_output[0:32]
authentication_key = kdf_output[32:64]
encryption_nonce = kdf_output[64:]
```

If context / domain separation is really important, it could be:
```
kdf_output = MAC("My-AEAD" || nonce, key, 64 + encryption_nonce_size)
```


This construction has the benefit of providing full nonce committement and nonce extension at the same time. It's also, to the best of my knowledge, the construction that requires the less computation when you need both context committement and nonce extension.

What do you think?

comments.author: samuel-lucas6
comments.body:
Hi, thanks for sharing your key derivation approach. I agree that a single call feels cleaner and is more performant. I've done that since writing this document (e.g., [this](https://github.com/samuel-lucas6/dissertation/blob/main/src/cAEAD/Proposals/Schemes/Nonce/cEtMBLAKE3.cs)). The subnonce approach is also fine when you have an XOF, but part of what motivated two calls was being restricted to a non-XOF and perhaps not a 512-bit output for two keys.

After hearing about [chacha20-blake3](https://github.com/skerkour/chacha20-blake3), I actually started drafting a blog post about generic composition for AEAD that touches on this but never finished due to other things happening.

Subkeys can either be static, nonce-based, or associated data (AD)-based, with these having different trade-offs. I like AD-based best because it's like the duplex and provides some level of misuse resistance (the key and nonce can be accidentally repeated if the associated data is different). This also means no concatenation/length encoding when computing a tag over the ciphertext/plaintext. Then the KDF ordering can allow static associated data to be cached for the same key. However, you need the associated data before encryption.

I think the domain separation is unnecessary for a generic construction like this but is arguably better practice.
